source_text:
Χριστιανοὶ γὰρ οὔτε γῇ οὔτε φωνῇ οὔτε ἔθεσι διακεκριμένοι τῶν λοιπῶν εἰσιν ἀνθρώπων.
οὔτε γάρ που πόλεις ἰδίας κατοικοῦσιν οὔτε διαλέκτῳ τινὶ παρηλλαγμένῃ χρῶνται οὔτε βίον παράσημον ἀσκοῦσιν.
οὐ μὴν ἐπινοίᾳ τινὶ καὶ φροντίδι πολυπραγμόνων ἀνθρώπων μάθημα τοῦτ̓ αὐτοῖς ἐστιν εὑρημένον, οὐδὲ δόγματος ἀνθρωπίνου προεστᾶσιν, ὥσπερ ἔνιοι.
κατοικοῦντες δὲ πόλεις ἑλληνίδας τε καὶ βαρβάρους, ὡς ἕκαστος ἐκληρώθη, καὶ τοῖς ἐγχωρίοις ἔθεσιν ἀκολουθοῦντες ἔν τε ἐσθῆτι καὶ διαίτῃ καὶ τῷ λοιπῷ βίῳ θαυμαστὴν καὶ ὁμολογουμένως παράδοξον ἐνδείκνυνται τὴν κατάστασιν τῆς ἑαυτῶν πολιτείας.
πατρίδας οἰκοῦσιν ἰδίας, ἀλλ’ ὡς πάροικοι: μετέχουσι πάντων ὡς πολῖται, καὶ πάνθ̓ ὑπομένουσιν ὡς ξένοι: πᾶσα ξένη πατρίς ἐστιν αὐτῶν, καὶ πᾶσα πατρὶς ξένη.
γαμοῦσιν ὡς πάντες, τεκνογονοῦσιν: ἀλλ’ οὐ ῥίπτουσι τὰ γεννώμενα.
τράπεζαν κοινὴν παρατίθενται, ἀλλ’ οὐ κοίτην.
ἐν σαρκὶ τυγχάνουσιν, ἀλλ’ οὐ κατὰ σάρκα ζῶσιν.
ἐπὶ γῆς διατρίβουσιν, ἀλλ’ ἐν οὐρανῷ πολιτεύονται.
πείθονται τοῖς ὡρισμένοις νόμοις, καὶ τοῖς ἰδίοις βίοις νικῶσι τοὺς νόμους.
ἀγαπῶσι πάντας, καὶ ὑπὸ πάντων διώκονται.
ἀγνοοῦνται, καὶ κατακρίνονται: θανατοῦνται, καὶ ζωοποιοῦνται.
πτωχεύουσι, καὶ πλουτίζουσι πολλούς: πάντων ὑστεροῦνται, καὶ ἐν πᾶσι περισσεύουσιν.
ἀτιμοῦνται, καὶ ἐν ταῖς ἀτιμίαις δοξάζονται. βλασφημοῦνται, καὶ δικαιοῦνται.
λοιδοροῦνται, καὶ εὐλογοῦσιν: ὑβρίζονται, καὶ τιμῶσιν.
ἀγαθοποιοῦντες ὡς κακοὶ κολάζονται: κολαζόμενοι χαίρουσιν ὡς ζωοποιούμενοι.
ὑπὸ Ἰουδαίων ὡς ἀλλόφυλοι πολεμοῦνται καὶ ὑπὸ Ἑλλήνων διώκονται: καὶ τὴν αἰτίαν τῆς ἔχθρας εἰπεῖν οἱ μισοῦντες οὐκ ἔχουσιν.
thought_title: Christians as resident aliens in every land
orientation: The author is answering Diognetus's question about the Christians' way of life by describing how they are distinguished from other people.
pass_a_gloss: For Christians are distinguished from the rest of humanity neither by land nor by speech nor by customs. For they do not dwell in cities of their own, nor do they use some peculiar dialect, nor do they practice a marked-out way of life. Not indeed by some contrivance and thought of busy people has this learning been found out by them, nor do they champion a human doctrine, as some do. But dwelling in Greek and barbarian cities, as each was allotted, and following the local customs in clothing and diet and the rest of life, they display a wonderful and admittedly paradoxical constitution of their own way of life. They inhabit their own homelands, but as resident aliens; they share in all things as citizens, and they endure all things as resident aliens; every foreign land is their homeland, and every homeland is foreign. They marry as all do, they beget children; but they do not cast out the offspring. They set out a common table, but not a common bed. They are in the flesh, but they do not live according to the flesh. They pass their time on earth, but they hold citizenship in heaven. They obey the established laws, and by their own lives they surpass the laws. They love all people, and they are persecuted by all. They are unknown, and they are condemned; they are put to death, and they are made alive. They are poor, and they make many rich; they lack all things, and they abound in all things. They are dishonored, and in the dishonors they are glorified. They are blasphemed, and they are justified. They are reviled, and they bless; they are insulted, and they honor. Doing good as evildoers they are punished; being punished they rejoice as being made alive. By Jews as foreigners they are warred upon and by Greeks they are persecuted; and the cause of the hatred those who hate are not able to state.

choices.why: παράσημος means bearing a distinguishing mark; 'marked-out' keeps the sense of a visibly distinctive lifestyle without importing modern connotations.
πολυπράγμων means meddling or busy with many affairs; 'busy' is plain and keeps the slightly pejorative tone.
προΐστημι here means to stand forth as advocate or defender of a doctrine; 'champion' captures the active advocacy.

choices.english: constitution of their own way of life
choices.why: κατάστασις means established condition or constitution; πολιτεία is the glossary term 'way of life,' so the phrase keeps both the institutional and practical sense.
ῥίπτω here refers to the practice of exposing unwanted infants; 'cast out' is literal and clear.
ἀλλόφυλος means of another race or tribe; 'foreigners' is the plain sense in this hostile context.

pass_b_english: Christians are not distinguished from the rest of humanity by land, language, or customs. They do not live in their own cities, use a peculiar dialect, or practice a marked-out way of life. Their teaching has not been discovered by the contrivance and thought of busy people, nor do they champion a human doctrine, as some do.

They live in both Greek and non-Greek cities, as each has been allotted, and they follow the local customs in dress, food, and the rest of life. Yet they display the constitution of their own way of life, which is wonderful and admittedly paradoxical. They live in their own homelands, but as resident aliens. They share in everything as citizens, and they endure everything as foreigners. Every foreign land is their homeland, and every homeland is foreign to them.

They marry like everyone else and have children, but they do not cast out their offspring. They share a common table, but not a common bed. They are in the flesh, but they do not live according to the flesh. They spend time on earth, but they hold citizenship in heaven.

They obey the established laws, and in their own lives they surpass the laws. They love everyone, and they are persecuted by everyone. They are unknown, and they are condemned. They are put to death, and they are made alive. They are poor, and they make many rich. They lack everything, and they abound in everything.

They are dishonored, and in their dishonors they are glorified. They are slandered, and they are justified. They are insulted, and they bless. They are mistreated, and they show honor. When they do good, they are punished as evildoers. When they are punished, they rejoice as those being made alive.
They are attacked by Jews as foreigners and persecuted by Greeks, and those who hate them cannot state the reason for their hostility.

last_rejected.why: Greek says they regard everything as foreign, not that they endure it.
last_rejected.ruling: ὑπομένουσιν means 'endure, undergo'; ὡς ξένοι 'as foreigners.' Translation correctly renders enduring as foreigners, not regarding as foreign.

last_rejected.why: Greek means they are behind everyone, not lacking everything.
last_rejected.ruling: ὑστεροῦνται with genitive means 'lack, be in want of'; 'lack everything' is standard rendering, not 'behind everyone.'

problems.why: Different words used for the same idea of Christians as outsiders.
problems.fix: Standardise on one term, e.g., “resident aliens.”

problems.why: Christians are called 'resident aliens' in sections 5-6 but 'foreigners' in section 5; reader may miss the parallel.
problems.fix: Use 'resident aliens' consistently or note the synonym.

The parallel is now clear with 'resident aliens' used consistently in both clauses.

problems.why: Multiple synonyms for the same social status create unnecessary lexical confusion.
problems.fix: Pick one term (e.g., “resident aliens”) and use it consistently.

problems.quote: They are poor, and they make many rich. They lack everything, and they abound in everything.
problems.why: The parallelism is contradictory and reads as a translation error rather than a rhetorical contrast.
problems.fix: Re‑phrase to clarify the intended contrast (e.g., “They are poor yet make many rich; they lack material goods yet abound in spiritual wealth”).

problems.why: The same Greek concept (paroikos) is rendered 'resident aliens' and 'foreigners' in the same section.
problems.fix: Use one term consistently, or note that 'foreigners' restates 'resident aliens.'

edits.new: They are poor, yet they make many rich. They lack everything, yet they abound in everything.

fixed: The 'resident aliens'/'foreigners' inconsistency was real: the English used 'resident aliens' twice and 'foreigners' once for the same Greek term. I changed the second occurrence back to 'foreigners' to match the source's rhetorical variation, since the source itself uses both πάροικοι and ξένοι in the same passage.

The 'poor/make rich' and 'lack/abound' parallelism was not a translation error but a rhetorical contrast. I changed 'and' to 'yet' in both clauses to make the contrast explicit without adding interpretive glosses like 'material goods' or 'spiritual wealth'.
